title: The heart's wish
hookLine: pooran hoe chit kee ichhaa: may my heart's longing be fulfilled, my mind rest at Your feet (Chaupai)

lines: THE LIST GETS SHORTER WITH AGE.
cards: Ask a child what they wish for and you'll get a list: a puppy, a bike, to stay up late. Ask a teenager and the list changes. Ask someone in their forties and it changes again.

Ask someone at the end of a long life and the list usually gets very short, often one or two things, almost never things you can buy. Underneath all the lists is a deepest wish, the one that rarely gets said out loud.
Chaupai's second line asks for exactly that wish to be fulfilled.

teach.b: The line is pooran hoe chit kee ichhaa. Pooran: full, complete, fulfilled. Chit: the mind, the heart, your inner awareness.
Ichhaa: wish, longing. May the wish of my heart be fulfilled. Sikh teaching is often wary of wanting.
The Guru Granth Sahib warns again and again about trishna, the thirst that never stops, the craving that eats a life. So how can Chaupai ask God to fulfill a wish? Because of the very next line.
In paraphrase: may my mind remain at your feet. The two lines come as a pair. The wish isn't the puppy or the bike.

It's the deepest one, to stay close to the One. In Sikh imagery, the feet are the place of humility and nearness, where you sit when you've stopped trying to be in charge. Later in the same prayer, the wish comes back.
In paraphrase: may my hope be fulfilled, and may my thirst for your praise remain. A prayer that asks for one thirst never to be quenched. Other cravings, the tradition says, leave a person emptier.

teach.h: WARY OF THIRST, YET ASKING A WISH.
teach.b: This one, as Sikhs read it, is the opposite: a thirst that fills while it stays a thirst.

teach.h: THE PAIR: MY MIND AT YOUR FEET.
teach.b: So the line isn't a blank check.
It's a question with an answer folded inside: what does your heart want, underneath the list?
Chaupai's answer is to stay at the feet, and to keep wanting that.

how: Many Sikhs recite these lines in Chaupai Sahib morning and evening, and they are often quoted in Sikh teaching as a prayer for the longing to stay near God.

o: a promise made in return for help
a wish, the heart's deepest longing
a blessing given at a wedding

games.q: the heart's wish — tap the pairs.

s: Chaupai asks God to grant any wish at all
the line is paired with the next: may my mind remain at your feet. that's the wish.
later in the prayer, it asks that one thirst never be quenched
may my thirst for your praise remain: the one thirst the prayer wants to keep.
Sikh teaching sees every kind of longing as good
the Guru Granth Sahib warns again and again about trishna, the craving that never stops.

games.q: you pray, may my heart's wish be fulfilled. what does Chaupai's very next line say the wish is?
o: may my mind remain at your feet.
games.why: the two lines are a pair. the heart's wish is to stay at the Lord's feet, the place of humility and nearness.

practice: Let the surface wishes come first, the things you want this week, this year, and let them pass like cars going by.
Then ask quietly what you want most underneath all of them, to be at peace, to be close to someone, to be close to God, to be good, and give it time.
When something feels true, name it in a few words; if you pray, offer it with Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Ichhaa, wish or longing. Pooran hoe chit kee ichhaa: may my heart's longing be fulfilled, paired with the line that names it, to stay at the Lord's feet.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: ichhaa, wish or longing; in Chaupai, the heart's wish that the next line names.

carryVoice: Your line: stay at the feet. One thirst worth keeping. Day three hundred seventy-two, done.

sources.ref: Benti Chaupai, verse with 'tor bhajan kee rahai piaasaa'
